Spatial distribution of Marine Heat Wave categories over Indian Ocean
The Indian National Centre for Ocean Information Services (INCOIS), a research organisation under the Ministry of Earth Sciences (MoES), has issued a Marine Heat Wave (MHW) warning across the Arabian Sea, the Indian Ocean and the Bay of Bengal. The warming conditions could adversely affect coral reef ecosystems, marine productivity and coastal biodiversity.
Six ocean basins
The intensity of the marine heat waves has largely been classified under the ‘Watch’ and ‘Alert’ categories, indicating sea surface temperature anomalies of up to 1 degree celsius above normal levels. The study area covered under this service is divided into six ocean basins, including the Persian Gulf, Red Sea, Southern Indian Ocean and South China Sea, as well as 14 sectors along the Indian coastline for detailed regional analysis.
What are scientists assessing?
Scientists are also assessing the intensity of marine heat waves and their potential impact on seagrass meadows, seaweed ecosystems and fisheries. These conditions could lead to biodiversity loss, shifts in species distribution and long-term ecological changes linked to climate change.
Swell surge warning for east and west coasts
INCOIS on Wednesday (November 4, 2026) has also issued a swell surge warning for both the east and west coasts for the next two days, including the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. A danger alert was issued for Car Nicobar Island. According to an official bulletin, waves of one metre or higher are expected to impact the coasts of Gujarat, Goa, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Kerala, Odisha, Andhra Pradesh, Lakshadweep, Puducherry, Tamil Nadu and West Bengal.

After days of storm action, the Gold Coast is officially trading its umbrellas for sunscreen as a mini heatwave moves in.
The wild weather has cleared out, making way for a weather shift that will see temperatures across the coast skyrocket into the low-to-mid 30s today.
According to the Bureau of Meteorology’s Jonathon How, tomorrow is shaping up to be the peak of the hot spell.
Coastal areas are bracing for sizzling top of 34 to 35 degrees, while inland suburbs could easily climb an extra degree or two higher as scorching winds sweep across Queensland.
“We are expecting temperatures on the coast to be about 34, 35 degrees and possibly one or two degrees warmer inland,” How said.
“We’ve got very hot wind coming through for inland parts of Queensland.
While the heat will be short-lived, the change heading into the weekend won’t bring total relief from the muggy conditions.

Skip to contentHeavy rain lashes Khammam, Bhadradri Kothagudem; red alert issued
HYDERABAD: Heavy rainfall battered Khammam and Bhadradri Kothagudem districts in Telangana over the 24 hours ending November 4, 2026, with several mandals recording more than 200mm of rain, according to rainfall data attributed to the Telangana Development Planning Society (TGDPS).
Mulakalapally in Bhadradri Kothagudem district recorded the highest rainfall in the supplied data at 231.8mm. Dammepeta also reported multiple high rainfall readings, including 214.3mm, 210mm and 198.3mm.
In Khammam district, Vemsoor recorded 196.5mm, followed by Sathupally at 188mm, Kalluru at 182.5mm and Penuballi at 178mm.
Red alert warns of extremely heavy rainfall
A red alert was issued for Bhadradri Kothagudem and Khammam districts for November 3 and 4, warning of heavy to extremely heavy rainfall in isolated locations.
Thunderstorms and intense downpours were also reported in areas including Dammepeta, Aswaraopeta, Mulakalapally, Chandrugonda, Kothagudem and Bhadrachalam.
Residents advised to remain alert over flood risk
The weather update warned that continued rainfall could trigger flash floods in low-lying areas and locations already receiving substantial rainfall.
Residents in vulnerable areas were advised to remain alert and follow official weather and disaster management advisories.
